post.message: Interesting...
Sean: thanks for concise and cogent impressions. I have just started dipping my toes in Clojure and Scala and appreciate frank, workaday takes on the languages.
Sean, thanks for the shout-out! Yours is honestly the best single summary of what Amanda and I were trying to convey I've seen. It's very gratifying!

First time I read a blog post from the future!

Great, Sean!

One remark: the code would get less complex IMHO if you just annotated
fibonacci :: [Long]
or
fibs :: Long -> Long -> [Long]

This way, you could save the conversions from and to Int.
And as the numbers grow rapidly, Long is better anyway!

Thanks for looking over the code. I'll update that... I just wanted to avoid type annotations except for the API but if annotating `fibs` is all it takes to make the whole thing work on `Long`, including the static method `fib`, that would be nicer. BTW, am I correct about the lack of stack overflow potential with the lazy recursive call? I read your post on the list and wondered if the deferred additions could cause a stack overflow when forced...

You can probably get away without any annotations when you write the integer constants with a trailing L.

Oh, I see now that you use the input Long as index, so we need to convert this to an Int (unless you use genericDrop from Data.List instead of drop), but we can still avoid holding the data as Ints, which will overflow rather quickly.

I guess the stack could overflow if you index into the list with a big enough index.
One way to avoid this would be to decorate the b argument of fibs with a bang. This would force calculation of (a+b) before the next list node is constructed.

If I annotate `fibs` as `Long -> Long -> [Long]`, it does indeed infer `Long` everywhere, but then I need to add a cast on the argument of `drop`:

fib n = head $ drop (Long.int n) $ fibonacci

You're also correct that defining:

fibonacci = fibs 0L 1L

let's me omit the annotation on `fibs` -- nice!

Good to know about `!` on `b`. Maybe I'll update the blog post to clarify that, one way or another.
You are so bad a55. Always impressed and inspired.

>haven’t really been able to get deeply into Python
Did you try Jython? I never tried it myself so I'm not sure how usable is it.
There was some SML for JVM too. :)

Ability to call Frege from Clojure is impressive, but what I find sad is that any FFIs are now limited to primitive types, or, at best, to method calls between languages with same object system.

Making an FFI algebraic type aware is surely a nontrivial task, but it's probably worth research. More and more languages pick up the idea (Scala, Rust, Swift...), but you still can't call say ML code from Haskell despite the absense of theoretical obstacles for doing so. Maybe with some language-agnostic constructor tag to int mapping files it can be done for languages that run on the same VM. Maybe we need a radically new OS design not centered around a language that was, from language theory point of view, born outdated. ;)

Jython was lagging far enough behind regular Python that I didn't want to waste time on it (and it wasn't clear how good the interop would be between Jython and other JVM languages since that's generally a pain point with languages that get _ported_ to the JVM instead of being written _for_ the JVM).

https://existentialtype.wor...

I've been interested in this dynamic vs static languages debate for a while now and I've consistently found that the static side has the better arguments...

Not really a relevant comment for this post but I decided to allow it anyway. I've read Harper's piece before (several times) and whilst there is some accuracy in trying to describe a dynamic type system as being a static type system with an "any" unitype, that really misses the point. Google for arguments against Harper's view - you'll find some really good insights into the value of dynamically typed languages.
I would say lambda's and Clojure are very closely related to the typing debate, but I suppose I'm no expert.

Lambdas appear in both statically typed and dynamically typed languages so that is why I felt a link to a "static vs dynamic" blog post was not really relevant.

Not sure what Clojure has to do with this either...?

What do you mean by "this" in the sentence "Not sure what Clojure has to do with this..."?

You can read your article above to see how they are related.

I meant in connection with your comments. You're not explaining yourself very well and you're neither asking any actual questions nor making relevant comments as far as I can see.

Can you perhaps elaborate on your point -- if you have one -- so that we can have an actual discussion?

Just that Java 8, with it's inclusion of lambda's, pushes the language toward the direction of less verbosity at the expense of clarity.

I see this situation as being closely related to types, as the same arguments are generally used for and against static vs dynamic languages.

I don't think that's an outrageous inference to make.

Ah, I see where you're coming from now! I'm not sure I'd agree with your assertion that verbosity vs clarity is the same argument used in the static vs dynamic languages discussion tho'...

Scala is much less verbose than Java but both are statically typed languages. Haskell -- which has been around a quarter century now! -- is also statically typed and much less verbose than Java. Static typing really has nothing to do with how verbose a language needs to be: Java's verbosity is due to its design and its very simplistic compiler. It's a nursemaid for an army of mediocre "enterprise" developers.

Most statically typed languages rely on type inference to avoid the need to write down the types. You can provide type annotations but generally you don't have to. Java requires type annotations and is often held up as "static typing is bad" but really it's "Java is bad".

I'd argue that Java's verbosity actually detracts from its clarity. I think code written in Scala / Haskell / Frege / Elm / PureScript / etc has much better clarity because it has less "noise" (I'll concede that very dense, obtuse code can be written in those languages, but I've seen dense, obtuse, and VERBOSE Java code too).

Arguing that dynamic languages and less verbose than static languages is not really valid. Nor that dynamic languages are "just" uni-typed static languages. Both of those miss the real benefit of a dynamic language: malleability. The ability to grow and evolve solutions "on the fly" is why developers move to dynamic languages.

Bear in mind that dynamic languages are nearly always still strongly typed: this isn't an issue of typed vs not-typed. Dynamic languages just trade off where the type checking is performed. The upside is the malleability, the downside is that you need to exercise code at runtime to ensure it type-checks. That means more tests -- larger test suites -- unless you have other language design features at play that reduce the need for testing (such as persistent, immutable data structures, and pure functions).

Java 8 has added some type inference in order to make functional idioms less painful to use -- anonymous functions don't need as much type annotation as "regular" Java code -- and they've introduced a number of "behind the scenes" type coercions so that "functional interfaces" can be automatically derived as needed. It's a good compromise, and why I think Java 8 is such an impressive step forward.

But it's still not functional enough for my tastes and that's why I prefer Clojure. Computations that are idiomatic (and efficient) in Clojure are still pretty ugly in Java -- and that has nothing to do with the type system per se.

I would probably have started using Haskell years ago if it ran on the JVM -- and that's why I'm interested in Frege these days (essentially Haskell for the JVM) and why I created lein-fregec as a way to mix Frege into my Clojure code. There's a benefit to having a static type system which can prevent whole classes of errors even getting into your code (no Null Pointer Exceptions!). Java doesn't have that benefit tho'...

Interesting perspective. I see the verbosity of Java as a feature, not a failure.
That's just a symptom of having a language that systematically describes the author's intent.
Though I agree that I would have preferred a language that didn't allow mutability at all..
Frege looks very cool, though I know next to nothing about functional programming except most people say it's very hard to read.

I think that depends on which "most people" you talk to. As part of ClojureBridge, we've had great success teaching Clojure to folks who are new to programming and they don't find it hard. However, people with (only) a strong OOP background really struggle with immutability (more so than the functional part) because they're so used to encapsulated state and mutating it to get anything done -- they focus on state and side-effects instead of behavior and data transformation.

When a functional language is taught as a first language, "most people" take to it really well -- and then find OOP fairly easy to pick up later. The reverse is not true, as OOP teaches some "bad thinking" that gets in the way of learning the functional principles. I base these observations on watching various people -- from complete newbies to seasoned developers -- learning new programming languages in a variety of courses both in-person and online over the last several years.

As for Java's verbosity, well, it's certainly a "feature" but no one is going to persuade me this sort of thing is a "good feature":

HashMap<string, arrraylist<string="">> m = new HashMap<string, arraylist<string="">>();

The complete -- and totally unnecessary -- duplication of type information on both sides?

And having to provide type information when it's obvious from the function signature:

Set<map.entry<string,arraylist<string>>> s = m.entrySet();

Writing that sort of nonsense is just soul-destroying :( Both left hand side annotations are inferable from the right hand side -- repeating them is just noise. The compiler knows the types involved -- it can (and should) keep track of that stuff for you.

Type inference (like Scala, Haskell, Frege, Elm, Rust, etc) really helps reduce that noise while maintaining type safety.
Thankyou Disqus for munging my Java code... hopefully you'll get the intent even tho' the syntax is now illegal :(

I don't think...
Ya, you don't have to declare the generics on both sides. I don't know what the ="" is for. (Edit: Oh lol, I see now.)
HashMap<string, arraylist<string="">> m = HashMap<>();
I think that changed with Java 8, though I don't know for sure. I remember plugging that in out of habit and then my IDE informed me I was being dumb.

I just wrote a program that creates Voronoi Diagrams and doesn't use any mutable classes or static fields, classes or methods (Except for builders) even though I see source code that leans on these things quite a lot.

I feel like you blame alot of the shortcomings of programmers on Java while at the same time championing languages that require more competence from the programmer.

Yeah, Disqus adds the = "" nonsense and lowercases all the types :(

It's possible (likely?) the type inference you indicate only came in with Java 8 -- which underlines my point that it's fundamentally unnecessary and could have gone away ages ago. Even so, you still need to repeat the top-level type (HashMap) which is still unnecessary.

"my IDE informed me I was being dumb" -- and that's another area where I get frustrated with Java and "Java developers": Java is so verbose that IDEs have evolved to provide code generation and all sorts of shortcuts to help developers avoid actual typing and to navigate monstrous codebases full of FactoryVisitorManager OOP nonsense. Anyway, that's a whole 'nother blog post :)

Do I think that Java has created a generation of dumb developers? Not entirely, but it has _enabled_ a generation of relatively unthinking developers. I see them asking all sorts of basic questions on forums that would have been unthinkable before "Enterprise Java" took hold. Yes, I do champion languages that require more competence. I think our industry as a whole has lowered the threshold, to our detriment: armies of less than mediocre programmers that can churn out millions of lines of dumb Java code, propped up by IDEs that do a lot of their "thinking" for them, does not improve our productivity or our quality.

Java is not a "good" language -- it is a "mediocre" language -- and the whole ecosystem is designed to support "mediocre" programmers (at best) so that they can churn out "solutions". I've sat in on conversations between these "Enterprise Java Developers" at Java conferences and hearing them talk about how they work, how they build software, makes me die inside a little every time.

Java 8 is a huge step forward -- for Java -- and it now allows for much more elegant solutions that competent developers can create. Hence my comment about it being "palatable". It's not going to change the direction of the super-tanker tho'. Armies of Java programmers will continue to churn out millions of lines of dumb Java code, just as before.

Better developers have moved on to better languages in general.

I suppose repeating "HashMap" is unnecessary in this case, but it's better programming to point to the interface anyway.
Map<string, arraylist<string="">> = new HashMap<>();
In that case it's not something that can or should be inferred.

I'd like to argue that Java developers are by-and large great programmers that use OOP in the way it was intended to create highly modular, maintainable, and concurrent code but that would be so laughably untrue I don't think the devil could advocate it.

Hell, I've had almost no formal education in Java, it's just a hobby of mine, and yet I'm sure there are legions of "Java Developers" that don't know what generics are, don't understand how statics harm their applications, don't know what a typing system is, and probably don't even know what "mutability" means.

http://blog.codinghorror.co...

The reality is, however, that these monkeys are cooking the spaghetti that "real programmers" have to come in and untangle down the line.

In my mind, that means the programming language is too flexible. We need to add more training wheels to this thing.

To you, it means we need to use languages that require the programmer to know what they're doing to just keep all the spaghetti at bay.

I can't really say that's wrong, but it does seem unrealistic to me.

As to "better languages" I suspect you're right. Paul Graham made an excellent point that you can always find problems with languages that are less "powerful" than the one you're using, but when you try to defend your language against other's that are more powerful one tends to just make rationalizations like "it's too hard to learn" or "I'm already good with language X".

I can point to problems in Javascript, Python, and C++ because they lack some feature or other, but I can't do the same thing with Lisp or functional languages because I simply don't know them. So can just resort to "They're weird and slow" with all the force of a wet noodle against a concrete slab.

http://www.paulgraham.com/a...

Amen to most of that -- and Paul Graham's writings are highly recommended (starting with that one). Also worth a read is Joel Spolsky's comments on "Java Schools":

http://www.joelonsoftware.c...

Part of the problem is that neither Java nor C++ are what was intended when OOP was "invented". OOP was supposed to be about autonomous "objects" that communicate by sending messages to each other. Instead we've built an industry on top of Java (and C++ and C#) that is considered "OOP" and, as you hint above, it's so far from what was intended that it would be laughable if it wasn't so soul-crushingly sad (and, oh, the billions it's cost us!).

I think our industry would do better with fewer people in it -- but better people, taught properly -- so I don't think "training wheels" are the answer. Beginners _can_ learn Haskell or Clojure or whatever. There's nothing inherently "complicated" about those languages or the concepts of FP on which they are built. The problem is how people are taught -- or at least the materials to which they are exposed. We almost need to burn down entire programming libraries to get rid of the bad stuff at this point. Sigh.

But well-taught programmers, with an aptitude for problem-solving, working in high-level languages -- and I mean higher than Java -- can be so much more productive than the armies of Java developers that inhabit corporate IT today.

Unrealistic? Yeah, you're probably right. But I can dream of a better future, eh? :)

Hey Sean, I know this is pseudo-unrelated to this conversation, but I wasn't sure how else to contact you.
I've been playing with Elm (Prodded somewhat by this conversatoin.) and what I noticed is that the structure of the programming is actually what the structure of a good Java program looks like (though less verbose.) and I'm definately seeing first hand what you were saying here.
Functional programming forces the programmer to do the things I wish people would do more of in Java and it's actually the very things I was thinking were designed to help the bad programmer that was actually enabling the bad behavior... Not defending against it.

However, there's also something else I'm noticing. Since everything in functional programming is immutable you can get away with swapping functions all over the place which is really cool first of all, but it also presents a situation where you're defining functions in some mysterious place and then pulling them out magically out of thin air and I'm not seeing a good way of tracking down where the implementation details of that function are coming from, nor is there an easy way to figure out what operations are available to me from a given library.

In Java, I could use my IDE to just right click and do a "show source" or manually follow an import.
In Elm there's constantly these functions that are being pulled out of a mysterious ass. For example;

http://elm-lang.org/edit/ex...
In there, I see "ngon", "filled", "collage", "move", and "toFloat"

Most of those are obvious in this case, but I can't immediately see where they are coming from, what they return, how they're implemented, or what other operations I can perform on a given returned function.

Sure, the type declaration's are certainly useful for figuring this stuff out, but it is tremendously easier to do in Java.

I think this is just a current limitation of Elm and not an inherent problem with Functional programming, is that right?

Wildcard imports are considered poor practice (but you often see them in toy examples). In any real code base, you'd either see specific imports (so the functions being imported would be itemized in the import itself) or aliases (so the import would create a short alias and you'd see that if every call).

A common example from Clojure is to (:require [clojure.string :as str]) and then you'll see (str/replace foo patt replacement) -- so it's obvious where replace comes from.

It doesn't look like my last reply went through...

This is kind of unrelated but I was playing with Elm somewhat in response to this conversation and I'm seeing some of my failings. The tools in Java that were meant to help the bad programmer do good code was actually enabling the bad behavior.
The kinds of things I'd like to see people do more in Java is absolutely enforced in functional programming.

There's one thing that's really annoying me though. Elm doesn't have an easy way of figuring out what's being returned, what functions can be performed on what's returned, what the implementation details of an imported function are, or even exactly where a function is being imported from (Sometimes).

"Learn the libraries" is certainly valid to a point but I definitely see room for a solid IDE to help the programmer navigate a codebase. This isn't an inherent problem of functional programming is it?

Here's a very simple example;
http://elm-lang.org/edit/ex...

Degrees, rotate, toForm, and show are all functions. Most of them I don't immediately know what they're accepting or returning. Can I replace "rotate (degrees 20)" with "scale 2"? (Turns out I can...) Can I replace it with "skew (90,90)"? Nope.

This makes me miss my builder patterns and step builder patterns. :l
I don't recognize that Clojure syntax, but the concepts make sense to me. Thanks.

Sean, do you have an example of this - "move all of our persistence from CFML’s “query” functionality to a Clojure “data mapper” based on clojure.java.jdbc."

I want to renew my effort to get into clojure. I went through a big chunk of "120 hours..." tutorial last year and didn't use any of it yet. Feel like I am loosing it all. I have a biggish project on FW1 with a lot of data. Is there a way to learn more about what problems Clojure helped you solve at world Singles?

Here's the CFML part of that equation: https://github.com/seancorf...

The Clojure part is called from that code and is a thin wrapper around the clojure.java.jdbc library (providing connection pooling for our data sources).

I've spoken at conferences and user groups about our use of Clojure so check out the Presentations page on my blog and I think there's a video of one of my talks up on InfoQ (from Clojure/West 2012?).

Hi,

I am curious why you decided to switch to boot after the two weeks spike. I don't see anything like a pros / cons list or some other facts. Could you please elaborate on what made you happy?

Thanks,
Sven

Per the benefits I list in the article:

* "the build script is straightforward executable Clojure, and tasks are just functions"
* "composability is baked right into the core of Boot"
* "having just a single JVM up and running was a win all round: every process started up faster, our task and automation code was simpler"

And "In the next blog post, I’ll talk about some of the specifics in our Boot infrastructure and the tasks we’re writing" -- so watch this space! :)
The next in the series: http://seancorfield.github....

I'm surprised to hear you aren't having any problem on Windows. Just a few days ago, based on your endorsement, I downloaded boot on Windows 10 and started working through the hoplon tutorial. Early in the tutorial, I started encountering errors and insurmountable problems. The boot guys don't use Windows, so there's really no support for that platform. I gave up.

Sounds like a problem with the Hoplon template / tutorial? I've had no problems while developing and testing boot-expectations or boot-new on Windows 10 - but I do all my World Singles work on OS X and deploy on Linux.
Thanks for providing more insights :-)

The same is valid for me on W7 and still, the number of issues for Windows just rises: https://github.com/boot-clj...
I have been concerned about that for over a year, but it seems like the boot folks are not interested yet in supporting windows.
Still, I like their approach. Well, however, we will see what the future brings.

Windows is not very friendly to tooling, to be honest. Leiningen was an appalling experience on Windows for a very long time and Boot was originally completely unusable on Windows. The Boot folks have been asking for help in fixing the Windows issues -- and Windows 7 causes problems that have gone away in Windows 10.

The vast majority of Clojure developers use OS X / Linux. If you want the Windows experience to get better, you're going to need to roll up your sleeves and debug the problems and submit Pull Requests to projects.

That said, I've successfully installed and used Boot for simple stuff on VMs running Windows 10, Windows 8.1, and Windows XP, as well as Windows 10 on my laptop. I just don't use Windows for any "real" development.

You are right in every regard. Actually, when they initially released boot I looked into it, saw the problems and thought about contributing, but decided against it for lukff reasons.

1. I think the design of boot relies too much on stuff that does not work on W7 like file locks and stuff. So changing that, might mean, I have to change the design, which I dont think I can do. Of course I might be wrong here, but, that was my impression.
2. I also tried to run the make script, but, like you said, they develop on Linux / OSX and so are their scripts, no sight of OS independence.

3. I just don't have the time to support a build tool on windows:

Also, I don't need boot, I just like fooling around with stuff. It's just as I said, the more projects switch to boot, the more people you will exclude.

And again, I don't want to be mean or anything, they are doing a great job, I just want to point at the consequences.

"I just don't have the time to support a build tool on windows:" -- I think this gets to the heart of the issue across the whole Clojure ecosystem. There just aren't enough Clojure developers using Windows who care enough about the experience to help make it better. We can debate the reasons for that but the bottom line is that until more Windows users decide to step up and help those project maintainers who only run OS X / Linux, the situation just isn't going to improve.

Folks for whom the tools work really well -- folks who, almost by definition, are not on Windows -- tend to not know enough about Windows to be able to make those tools work well on Windows. Although I've _used_ every version of Windows since 3.1, I've almost never _developed_ on Windows and I certainly don't understand enough of Windows' peculiarities to debug and fix problems I encounter there. Nor do I have much incentive to learn that much about Windows: I've always developed either on Unix or OS X and I've always targeted Unix / Linux for deployment.

Even back in the early 90's when I had Macs at home as my primary systems, I ran Tenon Intersystems' MachTen as a guest on them so I had a nice BSD Unix development environment.

I think Microsoft have steadily improved over the years in consumer-focused software: I even run Outlook as my primary email client on both iOS and OS X, for example. Windows has steadily improved too (well, excepting Windows ME and Vista!), and I used Windows 8 from early in the prerelease as a consumer O/S, moved to 8.1 as soon as that was available, and started using Windows 10 in prerelease about a year ago. Running Fast Ring Insider builds means I sometimes have to reinstall the O/S so I don't tend to get too invested in customizing that laptop and I certainly can't rely on it for anything more than a bit of hobby-level development in the evenings in front of the TV! Regarding the whole nilable thing, I have been thinking about optionality, and it seems to me that there are really two different "kinds" of optionality.

For example, a person may have a first, middle and last name, where middle name is “optional”. However, the absence of a :middle-name key in a map representing a Person is ambiguous and may have two different meanings: Either the information is absent, that is, we do not know in this context whether the person has a middle name, but it could also mean that the person does not have a middle name at all.

This is IMO an issue regarding the plans for spec. How would you spec a function that calculates the full name of a person? It would be incorrect to only require :first-name and :last-name. That would indicate that we do not need the middle name at all, which is incorrect - we do need the middle name if the person has one.

So in this situation, one might consider spec’ing :middle-name to be nilable. When the value is nil, the person does not have a middle name, and when the key is absent, it means that the information is absent in that particular context. The same considerations seem to apply to NULLs in databases.

I would argue that if you have a column that is "optional" because you don't know whether you have that data or not, you need an explicit piece of data for that, independent of the column itself. And that's exactly one of the things Rich called out in his talk -- don't complect "don't know" with "not present".

How do you avoid building/testing libraries/apps that were not changed (in a CI flow)? do you compute the graph of dependencies for each app in some way?

We can run a subset of tests based on just building a single app: we can compute the full set of dependencies based on transitively following :local/root dependencies between subprojects. We could use that to compute the downstream subprojects instead and just test/build anything that depends on what changed. But in reality the full test/build pipeline is fast enough for CI that it really doesn't matter and we haven't bothered to optimize it (yet). After all, if we make any changes to our "lower-level" subprojects, everything depends on them and so everything needs to be tested/built anyway (and the tests for those subprojects happen to be very fast so we wouldn't save much by not testing them).
